{
  "book_id": "gatsby",
  "notes": "The Great Gatsby is extraordinarily dense with signature material. Three main categories dominate: (1) culturally famous sentences and closing paragraphs that are among the most quoted in American literature; (2) Nick Carraway's voice-establishing passages — ironic digressions, satirical asides, and register-defining observations scattered throughout chapter middles that define the novel's moral and aesthetic consciousness; (3) interpretively weighted scenes and images that anchor critical readings (the green light, the eyes of Doctor Eckleburg, Daisy's voice as money, the Valley of Ashes). The downstream stage should hunt aggressively for: Nick's self-characterizing asides (his tolerance speech, his honesty claim, his birthday reflection); extended descriptive set-pieces (the parties, the Valley of Ashes, the Queensboro Bridge passage); dialogue exchanges that carry thematic weight (Gatsby on repeating the past, Daisy's voice full of money); and the novel's bookending philosophical meditations. Voice passages in chapter middles are especially at risk of compression loss.",
  "examples": [
    {
      "origin": "cultural",
      "category": "touchstone",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 1, opening paragraph",
      "passage_hint": "In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I've been turning over in my mind ever since.",
      "why": "The novel's famous opening sentence, establishing Nick's retrospective, morally self-conscious narration and the paternal advice framing device."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 1, early pages",
      "passage_hint": "Only Gatsby, the man who gives his name to this book, was exempt from my reaction—Gatsby, who represented everything for which I have an unaffected scorn.",
      "why": "Nick's paradoxical exemption of Gatsby from his general disgust is the novel's central critical crux, establishing the ambivalent admiration that structures the whole narrative."
    },
    {
      "origin": "cultural",
      "category": "quote",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 1, early pages",
      "passage_hint": "If personality is an unbroken series of successful gestures, then there was something gorgeous about him, some heightened sensitivity to the promises of life, as if he were related to one of those intricate machines that register earthquakes ten thousand miles away.",
      "why": "One of the novel's most celebrated characterizations of Gatsby, anchoring critical discussions of performance, selfhood, and the American dream."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 1, early pages",
      "passage_hint": "It was an extraordinary gift for hope, a romantic readiness such as I have never found in any other person and which it is not likely I shall ever find again.",
      "why": "The 'gift for hope' formulation is the novel's central characterization of Gatsby and returns in virtually every critical treatment of the book."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "voice",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 1, early pages — Nick's tolerance digression",
      "passage_hint": "Reserving judgements is a matter of infinite hope. I am still a little afraid of missing something if I forget that, as my father snobbishly suggested, and I snobbishly repeat, a sense of the fundamental decencies is parcelled out unequally at birth.",
      "why": "Nick's self-aware ironic qualification of his own tolerance is voice-defining and critically important as unreliable narrator setup."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "character",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 1, Tom Buchanan introduction",
      "passage_hint": "Two shining arrogant eyes had established dominance over his face and gave him the appearance of always leaning aggressively forward. Not even the effeminate swank of his riding clothes could hide the enormous power of that body—he seemed to fill those glistening boots until he strained the top lacing.",
      "why": "The novel's central characterization of Tom as embodied power and aggression; critics return to this passage for its class and masculinity themes."
    },
    {
      "origin": "textual",
      "category": "prosodic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 1, the Buchanan drawing room",
      "passage_hint": "A breeze blew through the room, blew curtains in at one end and out the other like pale flags, twisting them up toward the frosted wedding-cake of the ceiling, and then rippled over the wine-coloured rug, making a shadow on it as wind does on the sea.",
      "why": "A set-piece of Fitzgerald's impressionist prose style; the sustained wind imagery and sensory layering are textually distinctive and prosodically signature."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "voice",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 1, Daisy's voice description",
      "passage_hint": "It was the kind of voice that the ear follows up and down, as if each speech is an arrangement of notes that will never be played again. Her face was sad and lovely with bright things in it, bright eyes and a bright passionate mouth.",
      "why": "The novel's first extended treatment of Daisy's voice as object and instrument; anticipates the 'voice full of money' revelation and is a critical touchstone."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 1, closing scene",
      "passage_hint": "he stretched out his arms toward the dark water in a curious way, and, far as I was from him, I could have sworn he was trembling. Involuntarily I glanced seaward—and distinguished nothing except a single green light, minute and far away, that might have been the end of a dock.",
      "why": "The green light's first appearance, one of the novel's most symbolically loaded images; central to virtually every critical reading."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "structural",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 2, Valley of Ashes introduction",
      "passage_hint": "This is a valley of ashes—a fantastic farm where ashes grow like wheat into ridges and hills and grotesque gardens; where ashes take the forms of houses and chimneys and rising smoke and, finally, with a transcendent effort, of ash-grey men, who move dimly and already crumbling through the powdery air.",
      "why": "The Valley of Ashes is one of American literature's most analyzed symbolic landscapes; this passage is the locus classicus for readings of industrial waste and class."
    },
    {
      "origin": "cultural",
      "category": "touchstone",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 2, Doctor Eckleburg's eyes",
      "passage_hint": "the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg are blue and gigantic—their retinas are one yard high. They look out of no face, but, instead, from a pair of enormous yellow spectacles which pass over a nonexistent nose.",
      "why": "Among the most analyzed images in the novel; the eyes function as a godlike moral witness and are central to every major critical interpretation."
    },
    {
      "origin": "textual",
      "category": "voice",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 2, the party at the apartment — Nick's inside/outside observation",
      "passage_hint": "Yet high over the city our line of yellow windows must have contributed their share of human secrecy to the casual watcher in the darkening streets, and I saw him too, looking up and wondering. I was within and without, simultaneously enchanted and repelled by the inexhaustible variety of life.",
      "why": "'Within and without' is one of Nick's most quoted self-characterizations and a critical touchstone for his ambivalent observer role."
    },
    {
      "origin": "textual",
      "category": "prosodic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 3, Gatsby's parties description",
      "passage_hint": "In his blue gardens men and girls came and went like moths among the whisperings and the champagne and the stars.",
      "why": "A prosodically celebrated sentence; the 'moths' simile is among Fitzgerald's most anthologized images for its compression of the party world's beauty and transience."
    },
    {
      "origin": "textual",
      "category": "prosodic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 3, the party atmosphere",
      "passage_hint": "The lights grow brighter as the earth lurches away from the sun, and now the orchestra is playing yellow cocktail music, and the opera of voices pitches a key higher. Laughter is easier minute by minute, spilled with prodigality, tipped out at a cheerful word.",
      "why": "A sustained set-piece of Fitzgerald's synesthetic party prose; 'yellow cocktail music' is a signature phrase and the passage is prosodically unique."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "character",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 3, Nick meets Gatsby",
      "passage_hint": "He smiled understandingly—much more than understandingly. It was one of those rare smiles with a quality of eternal reassurance in it, that you may come across four or five times in life. It faced—or seemed to face—the whole eternal world for an instant, and then concentrated on you with an irresistible prejudice in your favour.",
      "why": "Gatsby's smile is among the novel's most critically discussed details; this extended description is the primary textual evidence for readings of Gatsby's magnetism and performed identity."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "voice",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 3, closing — Nick's honesty claim",
      "passage_hint": "Everyone suspects himself of at least one of the cardinal virtues, and this is mine: I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.",
      "why": "Nick's self-proclaimed honesty, placed ironically after the Jordan Baker dishonesty revelation, is a central crux for unreliable narrator readings."
    },
    {
      "origin": "textual",
      "category": "voice",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 3 middle — Nick on New York at night",
      "passage_hint": "I liked to walk up Fifth Avenue and pick out romantic women from the crowd and imagine that in a few minutes I was going to enter into their lives, and no one would ever know or disapprove.",
      "why": "A voice-establishing digression on Nick's urban fantasies that reveals his romantic imaginative life and his need for moral cover; at risk of compression loss."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "character",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 4, Gatsby's fabricated autobiography in the car",
      "passage_hint": "I am the son of some wealthy people in the Middle West—all dead now. I was brought up in America but educated at Oxford, because all my ancestors have been educated there for many years. It is a family tradition.",
      "why": "Gatsby's self-invention speech is a critical touchstone for American identity, self-fashioning, and the performative nature of the Gatsby persona."
    },
    {
      "origin": "textual",
      "category": "prosodic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 4, Queensboro Bridge passage",
      "passage_hint": "The city seen from the Queensboro Bridge is always the city seen for the first time, in its first wild promise of all the mystery and the beauty in the world.",
      "why": "A celebrated lyric moment in Nick's narration; the bridge passage is prosodically signature and appears in critical discussions of Fitzgerald's impressionism and New York as symbol."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 4, Jordan Baker explains Gatsby's plan",
      "passage_hint": "Gatsby bought that house so that Daisy would be just across the bay.",
      "why": "The revelation that collapses Gatsby's apparent wealth and grandeur into a single obsessive motive; interpretively essential for readings of the novel's romantic delusion theme."
    },
    {
      "origin": "textual",
      "category": "voice",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 4, Nick on Jordan Baker after the Central Park drive",
      "passage_hint": "There are only the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, and the tired.",
      "why": "A signature aphoristic formulation; widely quoted and critically noted as Nick's characteristic attempt to achieve moral distance through categorical thinking."
    },
    {
      "origin": "cultural",
      "category": "touchstone",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 5, Daisy and Gatsby reunion — the clock scene",
      "passage_hint": "He literally glowed; without a word or a gesture of exultation a new well-being radiated from him and filled the little room.",
      "why": "The reunion scene's emotional climax; Gatsby's 'glow' is a critical touchstone for the novel's treatment of romantic transformation and its limits."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 5, the green light speech",
      "passage_hint": "His count of enchanted objects had diminished by one.",
      "why": "The moment the green light loses its symbolic power once Daisy is present; a critical crux for readings of desire, idealism, and the impossibility of fulfillment."
    },
    {
      "origin": "cultural",
      "category": "quote",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 5, Gatsby's shirts scene",
      "passage_hint": "They're such beautiful shirts," she sobbed, her voice muffled in the thick folds. "It makes me sad because I've never seen such—such beautiful shirts before.",
      "why": "One of the novel's most analyzed and parodied scenes; Daisy's tears over shirts are central to every reading of materialism, desire, and Daisy's character."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 5, closing meditation on Gatsby's dream vs. reality",
      "passage_hint": "He had been full of the idea so long, dreamed it right through to the end, waited with his teeth set, so to speak, at an inconceivable pitch of intensity. Now, in the reaction, he was running down like an over-wound clock.",
      "why": "Nick's observation that the dream has outrun its object is the novel's central statement of the gap between imagination and reality; critically essential."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 6, Gatsby's origins — James Gatz",
      "passage_hint": "The truth was that Jay Gatsby of West Egg, Long Island, sprang from his Platonic conception of himself. He was a son of God—a phrase which, if it means anything, means just that—and he must be about His Father's business, the service of a vast, vulgar, and meretricious beauty.",
      "why": "The novel's most explicit statement of Gatsby as self-created myth; 'Platonic conception of himself' is among the most cited phrases in Fitzgerald criticism."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "narrative",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 6, Gatsby and Daisy's first kiss — the ladder image",
      "passage_hint": "Out of the corner of his eye Gatsby saw that the blocks of the sidewalks really formed a ladder and mounted to a secret place above the trees—he could climb to it, if he climbed alone, and once there he could suck on the pap of life, gulp down the incomparable milk of wonder.",
      "why": "The ladder image captures Gatsby's awareness that union with Daisy will end his solitary transcendence; a critical touchstone for the novel's treatment of romantic sacrifice."
    },
    {
      "origin": "cultural",
      "category": "quote",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 6, the first kiss",
      "passage_hint": "Then he kissed her. At his lips' touch she blossomed for him like a flower and the incarnation was complete.",
      "why": "The novel's most celebrated sentence about romantic idealization; 'incarnation' carries religious weight that critics consistently analyze."
    },
    {
      "origin": "cultural",
      "category": "quote",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 7, Daisy's voice as money",
      "passage_hint": "Her voice is full of money," he said suddenly. That was it. I'd never understood before. It was full of money—that was the inexhaustible charm that rose and fell in it, the jingle of it, the cymbals' song of it … High in a white palace the king's daughter, the golden girl …",
      "why": "One of the most quoted and analyzed passages in American literature; 'her voice is full of money' is the novel's central revelation about the relationship between love and wealth."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 6, Tom brings Gatsby's party under scrutiny",
      "passage_hint": "She was appalled by West Egg, this unprecedented 'place' that Broadway had begotten upon a Long Island fishing village—appalled by its raw vigour that chafed under the old euphemisms and by the too obtrusive fate that herded its inhabitants along a shortcut from nothing to nothing.",
      "why": "Nick's analysis of Daisy's reaction to West Egg is central to class-reading interpretations and to understanding the East Egg / West Egg distinction as cultural hierarchy."
    },
    {
      "origin": "cultural",
      "category": "quote",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 6, Gatsby on the past",
      "passage_hint": "Can't repeat the past?" he cried incredulously. "Why of course you can!" He looked around him wildly, as if the past were lurking here in the shadow of his house, just out of reach of his hand.",
      "why": "Among the novel's most quoted exchanges; Gatsby's belief in repeating the past is the thematic center of the book and of its critical reception."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "voice",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 7, Nick's thirtieth birthday",
      "passage_hint": "I was thirty. Before me stretched the portentous, menacing road of a new decade … Thirty—the promise of a decade of loneliness, a thinning list of single men to know, a thinning briefcase of enthusiasm, thinning hair.",
      "why": "Nick's birthday meditation links personal mortality to the novel's broader themes of time and loss; the ironic self-deprecation is voice-defining."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "character",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 7, Tom and Daisy after the accident",
      "passage_hint": "They were careless people, Tom and Daisy—they smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their money or their vast carelessness, or whatever it was that kept them together, and let other people clean up the mess they had made.",
      "why": "The novel's moral verdict on Tom and Daisy; this passage is the critical locus for readings of class privilege and irresponsibility."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "narrative",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 7, Wilson equates Eckleburg's eyes with God",
      "passage_hint": "I took her to the window—and I said 'God knows what you've been doing, everything you've been doing. You may fool me, but you can't fool God!' Standing behind him, Michaelis saw with a shock that he was looking at the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg.",
      "why": "The explicit equation of the billboard eyes with divine judgment is the novel's most direct statement of its moral-symbolic framework; critical touchstone for religious and symbolic readings."
    },
    {
      "origin": "textual",
      "category": "prosodic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 8, Gatsby's final vigil described retrospectively",
      "passage_hint": "He must have looked up at an unfamiliar sky through frightening leaves and shivered as he found what a grotesque thing a rose is and how raw the sunlight was upon the scarcely created grass.",
      "why": "A prosodically distinctive passage imagining Gatsby's final consciousness; the estrangement of familiar things (rose, sunlight) is a signature Fitzgerald effect, much analyzed."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 8, Nick's parting words to Gatsby",
      "passage_hint": "They're a rotten crowd," I shouted across the lawn. "You're worth the whole damn bunch put together.",
      "why": "Nick's only direct compliment to Gatsby, placed just before his death, is a critical crux for the novel's moral evaluation of Gatsby despite disapproving of him."
    },
    {
      "origin": "cultural",
      "category": "touchstone",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 9, closing meditation — the boats against the current",
      "passage_hint": "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.",
      "why": "The novel's last sentence is one of the most famous closing lines in American literature; central to all critical readings of time, dream, and the American condition."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 9, the fresh green breast of the new world",
      "passage_hint": "gradually I became aware of the old island here that flowered once for Dutch sailors' eyes—a fresh, green breast of the new world. Its vanished trees, the trees that had made way for Gatsby's house, had once pandered in whispers to the last and greatest of all human dreams.",
      "why": "The novel's expansion from Gatsby's personal dream to the American dream as historical tragedy; a critical set-piece for readings of Fitzgerald and national mythology."
    },
    {
      "origin": "critical",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 9, Nick on the West",
      "passage_hint": "I see now that this has been a story of the West, after all—Tom and Gatsby, Daisy and Jordan and I, were all Westerners, and perhaps we possessed some deficiency in common which made us subtly unadaptable to Eastern life.",
      "why": "Nick's retrospective reframing of the novel as a Western story is interpretively crucial for geographic and national readings of the text."
    },
    {
      "origin": "textual",
      "category": "voice",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 9, the owl-eyed man at the funeral",
      "passage_hint": "He took off his glasses and wiped them again, outside and in. 'The poor son-of-a-bitch,' he said.",
      "why": "The owl-eyed man's epitaph for Gatsby is the novel's most economical and moving elegy; its bluntness against the surrounding elegiac prose is prosodically and emotionally signature."
    },
    {
      "origin": "interpretive",
      "category": "thematic",
      "segment_hint": "Chapter 9, Gatsby's green light and the orgiastic future",
      "passage_hint": "Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgiastic future that year by year recedes before us. It eluded us then, but that's no matter—tomorrow we will run faster, stretch out our arms further … And one fine morning—",
      "why": "The novel's penultimate paragraph universalizes Gatsby's dream into a statement about human desire and temporal impossibility; one of the most interpreted passages in American literature."
    }
  ]
}
